title: A map of the world in squares
teaches: Tile pyramids, how many tiles each zoom needs, pre-rendering against rendering on demand, vector tiles, and versioned map updates

blocks.text: On 8 February 2005 Google opened Google Maps. Online maps already existed; on MapQuest, the most used, you clicked an arrow at the edge of the map and the whole page reloaded with a new picture shifted half a screen over. On Google's map you took hold of the image and dragged it, and it slid under the pointer, with new territory appearing at the edges as fast as you could pull. It came from Where 2 Technologies, a small company founded in Sydney by the brothers Lars and Jens Rasmussen with Noel Gordon and Stephen Ma, which Google had bought the October before.[^ajax]

The map worked this way because it was not one single image. The engineers had cut the world, at every zoom level, into square images 256 pixels on a side, called **tiles**, and the page asked the server for whichever tiles were in view, plus a border of tiles just outside the frame. As you dragged, JavaScript fetched the next squares in the background and placed them beside the ones already loaded. Each tile was a standard image file at a static URL, so every browser cache and every proxy cache between the browser and Google could keep a copy.

In this lesson, we will answer the design questions that follow from this architecture. How many squares does the whole world need, down to the zoom where you can see the lanes on a road? Which of them should we render ahead of time, and which only when a user first requests them? And when a road opens, how do we update a map stored across a billion cached squares? Here we begin the Maps and places branch, lessons M1 to M4, where we examine the systems behind an online map: its tiles, finding the nearest car, route planning and live traffic. Engineers at OpenStreetMap, the open map Steve Coast started in the UK in 2004, solve these same problems in public, and we will look at their designs below.

First we must project the globe onto a square. Web maps use the **Web Mercator** projection, which wraps the globe onto a cylinder, unrolls it, and cuts it off at about 85° north and south, where the stretched polar regions would make the map taller than it is wide.[^mercator] At **zoom** 0 the whole square is one tile. At each zoom level after that, every tile is quartered, so zoom *z* is 2^*z* tiles across and 2^*z* tiles down, or 4^*z* tiles in all. We name a tile by three numbers: its zoom, its column and its row. For example, 14/2624/5722 is the zoom-14 tile containing downtown Seattle, and the server builds the tile's URL directly from those three numbers.

We can calculate the resolution at each level. At zoom 0 the 40,075 km of the equator are spread over 256 pixels, giving about 157 km per pixel. Each zoom level halves that distance. Zoom 10 is about 150 metres per pixel, enough to show a town. Zoom 18 is about 60 cm per pixel, which is detailed enough to show the lanes of a road.

blocks.caption: The tiles at each zoom. The square on the left shows the grid up to zoom 6 and the tile that holds Seattle; the bars count the tiles at each zoom, with each line on the logarithmic scale representing ten times the count of the line below it.
blocks.task: Guess, then go down to zoom 18

blocks.text: Zoom 18 alone has 4^18 tiles, which is about 69 billion tiles, and every zoom from 0 to 18 together totals about 92 billion tiles. The sum is a third more than the deepest level alone, because each level holds a quarter as many tiles as the next deeper one. At 20 KB per tile, a typical size for a compressed map image, pre-rendering all of them would take nearly 2 petabytes of storage, even before counting the zoom levels beyond 18 that phones now use. Rendering every tile at every zoom in advance is therefore impractical.

parts.title: What to draw ahead of time

blocks.text: Users never view most of those tiles. About 71% of the Earth's surface is sea, and a deep-zoom tile of open ocean is a plain blue square. A tile store can keep one copy of that square and point every ocean address at it. Of the land, most is desert, ice, forest and farmland that users rarely zoom into. Traffic concentrates instead on cities and roads, and on the zoom levels people use to find a street or a neighbourhood. Tile popularity follows the same skewed distribution as the video traffic in lesson 19's edge caches, where a small fraction of the tiles receives most of the requests.

Because of this skew, engineers split the pyramid. The low zoom levels contain few tiles and every user views them, so we pre-render and store them ahead of time. We render the deep zoom levels on demand the first time a user requests one, which takes about 50 ms of compute time for a land tile, and then we store and cache the result. OpenStreetMap's tile servers operate this way. When a user requests an unrendered tile, the server renders it on demand alongside its neighbours in a block of 8 by 8 tiles, since rendering one block takes little more CPU time than rendering a single tile.[^metatile]

blocks.caption: Where to draw the line between tiles rendered ahead of time and tiles rendered on demand. The distribution of requests across zooms is an illustrative but typical curve; the storage and compute time follow from the tile counts at 20 KB and 50 ms per land tile.
blocks.task: Move the line down to zoom 18 and read the cost

blocks.text: With the cutoff at zoom 12 there are 22 million tiles, of which about 6.7 million contain land. At 20 KB for each land tile and one shared copy of the blue square for the ocean, storing them takes about 130 GB. We can render that set in minutes on a thousand CPU cores, and those tiles serve about a quarter of all requests. Each additional zoom level multiplies the storage and compute cost by four while covering a smaller share of requests. Rendering tiles on demand adds latency for the first viewer, but only the first, because the caching hierarchy from lesson 19 serves every subsequent request: the browser's local cache, the content delivery network (CDN) edge servers near the user, and finally the origin tile store. A screen of 1,920 by 1,080 pixels displays about 40 tiles, and dragging loads a few dozen more, so a high-traffic map service delivers hundreds of thousands of tiles a second, nearly all served from caches.

Maps change every day as roads open, shops close and names are corrected. A change appears on one tile at each zoom level where it is visible, or on two or four tiles if it sits near an edge, so a single edit invalidates about one tile per zoom level. We find the affected tiles with simple geometry: we take the edit's bounding box, widen it by the largest line width or label rendered around it, and list the tiles it overlaps at each zoom. A new map version re-renders only those modified tiles and points every other tile address at the previous version's image, so an update costs only the compute required for the changes. Low zoom levels change constantly because each tile covers a huge area, so engineers re-render those tiles in batch jobs, the kind of workload lesson 8's MapReduce was built for.

Invalidating the caches is harder. A tile served at a fixed URL may sit in a million browser caches and thousands of CDN edge caches, each retaining the file until its time-to-live (TTL) header expires. Sending a purge request to every edge server is slow and unreliable, and we cannot purge a user's browser cache at all. Furthermore, a partially updated map causes visual bugs: a new road rendered on one tile and missing from the cached tile beside it stops dead at the boundary.

To solve this, we never overwrite a tile at an existing URL. Instead, we embed a **version** number for the whole map in every tile's URL. A tile at a given version never changes, so caches can store it indefinitely.[^immutable] We render each new version of the map alongside the old one, and once the build completes, we update a small metadata file that tells client pages the current version number. We serve that metadata file with a TTL of about a minute, while the tiles themselves carry a TTL of a year. Client pages then request the new URLs, and the old tiles receive no further traffic and are eventually evicted from the caches.

blocks.caption: A versioned tile URL. Caches never need to be purged because a new version generates new URLs.

blocks.text: This versioning scheme causes a cold-cache spike. When the version number increments, every CDN edge cache misses on every tile request at once, and the origin tile store absorbs a surge of traffic until the caches warm up again. To reduce this load, engineers roll out new versions every few days rather than on every edit, and pre-warm the edge caches with popular tiles before switching the metadata file. We must also apply the same version number to the road graph used by lesson M3's route planner, so the map never displays a road that the routing engine cannot use.

A raster tile is a bitmap image: the server determines every colour, line width and label during rendering, and the client device simply displays the file. If the user rotates the map, the text labels turn upside down. If a user wants a dark theme at night, or labels in another language, the server must render and store an entire duplicate pyramid.

In December 2010 Google Maps 5.0 for Android began rendering maps on the phone from **vector** data. The tiles carried the geometry of roads, coastlines and buildings, and the client device rendered them locally, allowing the user to tilt the map into 3D and rotate it while keeping the labels upright. Mapbox published an open specification for vector tiles in 2014 that is now an industry standard. Each vector tile holds the geometric shapes that fall inside its boundary, clipped at the edges, with coordinates quantised as integers on a 4,096 by 4,096 grid, delta-encoded from the previous point and serialised in Protocol Buffers. The phone renders the geometry using a style sheet downloaded once from the server. Each tile also includes a buffer margin of geometry extending slightly past its boundary, ensuring that a road crossing a tile edge renders cleanly on both sides and allowing the label placement algorithm to avoid clipping text across boundaries.

Vector tiles shift the rendering workload from the server's storage and CPUs to the client's processor and GPU. Vector tiles are typically a fraction of the byte size of equivalent raster images, a single tile supports every visual style and language, and the client can scale a tile smoothly beyond its native zoom level. Because of this scaling, many vector map services stop generating new tiles at zoom 14 or 15 rather than zoom 18, reducing the total tile count by a factor of four for each omitted level. This compression makes whole regions small enough to download for offline navigation. The trade-off is that every client application must bundle a rendering engine with font shaping and label collision detection, older devices may drop frames while rendering, and the server gives up pixel-exact control over the display.

blocks.caption: Map tiles on the web, from OpenStreetMap's start in 2004 to an open specification for vector tiles in 2014.
Six questions on map tiles
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: How many tiles are there at zoom 10 of a web map, where each zoom splits every tile into four?
items.why: Zoom 10 is 2^10 = 1,024 tiles across and 1,024 tiles down, which is 1,048,576 tiles in all.

items.ask: Why do tile services pre-render the low zoom levels ahead of time, but render the deepest zoom levels only when first requested?
choices: Deep-zoom tiles change too often to be worth storing, while low-zoom tiles hardly ever change
Deep-zoom tiles are drawn by the browser from low-zoom ones, so the server only stores the low ones
Low zooms are few and seen by everyone; deep zooms are vast in number and mostly never viewed
items.why: Each zoom level has four times the tiles of the level above it, and most deep tiles cover sea, desert or farmland nobody views closely. Rendering on first request and caching the output spends compute resources only where users look.

items.ask: A map provider embeds the map's version number in every tile's URL. What is the advantage of this design?
choices: A tile never changes at its address, so caches keep it indefinitely and an update needs no purge
Old tiles are deleted from every browser and edge cache the moment a new version is published
Each tile can be updated on its own the moment an edit touches it, without waiting for others
items.why: Updated map content receives new URLs, so cached tiles are never stale; old tiles stop receiving requests and are evicted over time. The client requests all tiles from a single version, ensuring adjacent tile edges match.

items.ask: What is the cost of switching every tile request to a new version's URL at once?
choices: Readers see tiles from two versions mixed on one screen until their browsers restart
Every cache misses on every tile at first, so the tile store takes a surge until caches refill
The tile store must keep both versions for ever, doubling its storage after each release
items.why: New URLs are uncached across all edge servers and browsers. That is why engineers update map versions every few days rather than on each edit, and pre-warm popular tiles before switching versions.

items.ask: What workload do vector tiles shift from the server to the client device?
choices: The map data itself: the device stores the whole world and asks the server for nothing
The tile cutting: the device splits one large image into squares as needed
The drawing: the device turns geometry into pixels with a style it holds
items.why: The server sends geometric shapes rather than bitmap images. A single vector tile supports any visual style, language or rotation, at the cost of running a rendering engine on the client processor.

items.ask: Storing every tile from zoom 0 to 18 as a separate 20 KB image would require roughly how much storage?
items.why: Zooms 0 to 18 contain about 92 billion tiles, and 92 billion × 20 KB is about 1.84 PB if every tile is stored as a distinct file. Deduplicating the plain ocean squares, as described in part 3, eliminates most of that storage.

summary: **A web map is a pyramid of square tiles.** Zoom z has 4^z tiles of 256 by 256 pixels, each addressed by zoom, column and row.
**Each zoom level multiplies the tile count by four.** Zoom 18, at a resolution of about 60 cm per pixel, contains about 69 billion tiles.
**Pre-render the few low zooms and render the deep zooms on demand.** Most deep tiles cover ocean or unpopulated land that users rarely view.
**Request popularity is skewed, so caches serve most of the traffic.** Browser caches, CDN edge caches and the tile store serve a rendered tile to all subsequent viewers.
**Never overwrite a tile at an existing URL.** Embedding a map version in every tile's URL allows caches to retain tiles indefinitely and eliminates cache purges during updates.
**Switching versions causes a cache cold start.** Every cache misses when URLs change, so engineers release new versions every few days rather than with every edit.
**Vector tiles transmit geometry instead of bitmap images.** The client device renders them in any style or orientation, requiring a rendering engine on every client.

ajax.title: A name for the pattern
ajax.text: Ten days after Google Maps launched, the designer Jesse James Garrett published an essay naming this web architecture Ajax: pages that fetch data in the background with JavaScript and update the document without a full page reload. He cited Google Maps and Google Suggest as his primary examples.

mercator.title: Why 85 degrees
mercator.text: Mercator's projection stretches distances increasingly toward the poles, reaching infinity at 90° latitude. Truncating the map at about 85.05° north and south makes the projected world equally tall and wide, forming a square that divides cleanly into quadtree tiles. The trade-off is that the polar regions are omitted and high-latitude landmasses like Greenland appear as large as Africa.

metatile.title: Metatiles
metatile.text: Rendering a map requires querying the database for every road, label and coastline in the bounding box, including a margin beyond the tile's edge to place labels that cross boundaries. Rendering a block of 8 by 8 tiles as one large image and slicing it into 64 individual tiles amortises the database query across all 64 tiles and prevents text labels from being clipped at tile edges.

immutable.title: Caching indefinitely
immutable.text: An HTTP response can include the header Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable, which instructs caches to retain the file for 31,536,000 seconds (one year) without revalidating it with the origin server. This is safe only when the content at a URL never changes, which versioned URLs guarantee.
